podcast.title: Purchase of the "Black Strat" (1969)
podcast.body: David Gilmour's renowned "Black Strat," the legendary guitar used on many iconic Pink Floyd recordings, was purchased at Manie's Music in 1969. This acquisition highlights the store's importance as a source for significant musical instruments. "David Gilmore's famous Black Strat, the legendary guitar, used on so many iconic Pink Floyd recordings, was purchased at Manie's in 1969."

podcast.title: Auction Sale of the "Black Strat"
podcast.body: David Gilmour's legendary "Black Strat" was eventually sold at auction for nearly $4 million US dollars. The purchaser was Jim Irsay, who is the owner of the Indianapolis Colts. "It sold at auction for nearly $4 million US dollars to Jim Isray, the owner of the Indianapolis Colts."

podcast.title: Roadie for Pink Floyd, then Member
podcast.body: In the mid-1960s, David Gilmour initially worked as a roadie for Pink Floyd. He was later invited to join the band as a guitarist by drummer Nick Mason, marking his transition from support staff to a full-fledged member. "Way back in the mid 1960s David Gilmore roadied for a young band called Pink Floyd. He was drummer Nick Mason who invited him into the band as a guitarist."

podcast.body: David Gilmour's iconic "Black Strat" was purchased at Mani's Music in New York in 1970. This specific guitar became a cornerstone of his sound, being utilized for every Pink Floyd album and tour following its acquisition. "David Gilmore's beautiful solo on Pink Floyd's comfortably numb was played on his famous Black Strat, a guitar he bought at Mani's Music in New York in 1970."

xref.title: Nash the Slash (Jeff Plunman, Toronto, 1948–2014) – Surgical Bandages Adopted After Three Mile Island Accident (1979); David Gilmour Offered Guitar Part but Nash Refused All Guitars
xref.body: Nash the Slash's real name was Jeff Plunman, born in Toronto on March 26, 1948. The stage name came from a character in a 1927 Laurel and Hardy silent film. He co-founded the prog band FM in 1975 and audiences could see his face briefly, but after the nuclear accident at Three Mile Island near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania in March 1979, Nash adopted surgical bandages that completely obscured his face as a way of raising awareness about what could happen if a nuclear plant melted down. He left FM around 1980 to resume his solo career, toured with Gary Numan and the Tubes, hung out with Iggy Pop and Daniel Lanois, and Brian Eno collaborated on his records. David Gilmour of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs — but Nash refused because he never used guitars on any of his songs. He made records until 2012, was especially popular in Germany and Poland, and died of an apparent heart attack at his Toronto home on May 10, 2014, at age 66. His music and costumes are managed by the Nash the Slash Legacy organization and much was donated to the National Music Center in Calgary. His best-known record was 1984's American Bandages. "David Gilmore of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs, but Nash refused because he never, ever used guitars on any of his songs."

xref.title: Discovery by David Gilmour
xref.body: At the age of 14, Kate Bush was discovered by David Gilmour of Pink Floyd. He immediately recognized her distinct talent, as she was already playing piano, violin, and organ, and writing her own songs. Gilmour took her demo tape to EMI Records, Pink Floyd's label. "David Gilmore of Pink Floyd, chanced upon a 14 year old girl who had been playing piano, violin, and organ as well as writing her own songs."

xref.title: Early Life and Musical Influences – Childhood to Age 11
xref.body: John Frusciante was born in Queens, New York, into a very musical family. His family moved multiple times, including to Tucson, Florida (where his dad was a judge), Santa Monica, and finally Los Angeles after his parents' divorce. His stepfather greatly encouraged his musical interests. His initial passion was for punk rock band The Jirms, which used unusual punk rock tuning. By age 11, he was studying the styles of David Gilmour, Jimi Hendrix, Jimmy Page, Jeff Beck, and Frank Zappa, eventually convincing his parents to let him drop out of high school to study music full time. "He was so into guitar that he convinced his parents that he should drop out of high school and let him study music full time."

xref.title: Early Musical Development and Discovery
xref.body: Kate Bush began teaching herself piano at age 11, and by age 15, she was discovered by Pink Floyd's David Gilmour, a family friend. At this point, she also played violin and organ and had started writing her own songs, leading to a 50-track demo and a subsequent signing with EMI, coincidentally Pink Floyd's label. "Starting at the piano at age 11, she taught herself, she was discovered by Pink Floyd's David Gilmore when she was 15."
